lead: A Linux computer separates power. The kernel is the privileged core that owns the hardware: it schedules processes, manages memory, and talks to disks and network cards. Everything else, including the shell you type into, runs in user space with limited rights. The shell is an ordinary program: it reads a command line, starts other programs, and asks the kernel to act through system calls. This split is why one bad program rarely crashes the machine, and why a small shell can control a large system. You meet it every time you type a command.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for Unix and Linux history and Chapter 1.2 for multi-user, multitasking and modular kernel ideas.

blocks.text: The CPU has at least two privilege levels. In kernel mode, code can execute every instruction and touch every memory address. In user mode, code is restricted: it cannot directly read a disk or change page tables. The kernel runs in kernel mode. Your programs run in user mode. A mode bit in the CPU status register decides which level is active; a trap or interrupt switches the CPU into kernel mode.

The kernel is the part of the operating system that stays in memory. It schedules which process runs on the CPU, manages virtual memory and page tables, runs device drivers, and provides system calls. A system call is a controlled entry point from user mode to kernel mode. Examples are open, read(2), write, fork and execve. User code puts a system-call number and arguments in registers, then executes a trap instruction. The CPU switches to kernel mode, the kernel checks the request, does the work, and returns to user mode.

The layers are simple to draw. Hardware is at the bottom: CPU, RAM, disk and network card. The kernel sits above it in privileged mode. The system-call boundary is the gate between modes. User programs sit above that gate: the shell, utilities such as ls and vi, and applications such as a browser.

sections.h3: The shell is an ordinary user program

blocks.text: The shell is a command interpreter. It prints a prompt, reads a line from the terminal, parses it into words, performs expansions, and decides what to run. bash, zsh and sh are shells. None is part of the kernel. When you type ls, bash does not read the directory itself. It searches the directories listed in PATH, an environment variable, finds /bin/ls, starts it as a child process, and waits.

The shell resolves a command line in this order: alias, reserved word or keyword such as if and while, function, built-in, then an external file found in PATH. The common cases are four. A shell built-in runs inside the shell process, so it can change the shell's own state; cd and export are built-ins. An external command is a separate program file such as /bin/ls. An alias is a shell shortcut for another command line. A function is a named block of shell commands. For an external command, the shell calls fork to make a child and execve to load the program. fork and execve are system calls, so the kernel performs them, but the decision to call them is made by the shell in user mode.

Utilities are separate programs too: ls, cp, grep, vi and your browser all live in user space. They use the same system-call boundary. A new utility does not need a new kernel. A faulty editor usually dies without stopping the kernel. The shell plus utilities form the user-visible command line; the kernel remains the shared foundation underneath.

The boundary gives protection and stability. A user process cannot write to another process's memory or to raw disk blocks unless the kernel allows it. The kernel checks every request: file permissions, memory addresses, device access. If a program divides by zero or dereferences a bad pointer, the CPU raises a fault; the kernel may kill that process, but other processes and the kernel keep running.

The cost is overhead. Each system call switches mode and copies small amounts of data. Programs batch reads and writes instead of asking the kernel for one byte at a time. The split also makes the shell replaceable: you can run bash, dash or zsh on the same kernel. A distribution packages a kernel with libraries, shells and utilities; see Chapter 1.5. The simple rule: the kernel is privileged and shared; the shell is unprivileged and yours.

examples.question: A user types ls and presses Enter in bash. Trace the steps: shell parses the line; shell starts /bin/ls; ls makes system calls; the kernel returns directory bytes and ls prints. Which steps run in user mode and which in kernel mode? Name the two user processes.
steps: bash is in user mode. It calls read(2) on the terminal; the kernel's terminal driver runs in kernel mode, takes the bytes for the line ls, and returns them to bash. bash parses the line into one word, ls, expands no variables, and sees that ls is not a built-in. Still user mode.

bash searches PATH, finds /bin/ls, and calls fork. The kernel runs in kernel mode to create a child process. fork returns 0 in the child and the child's process ID (PID) in bash. bash calls waitpid and sleeps.

The child calls execve('/bin/ls', argv, envp). By convention argv[0] is the command name ls, the remaining entries are the arguments, and envp holds environment strings of the form NAME=value. The kernel runs in kernel mode, checks the file, replaces the child's memory image with the ls program, and returns to user mode at the entry point of ls. The process keeps the same PID.

ls runs in user mode. It calls open and read(2) on the directory; each call traps to the kernel, where the file system and disk driver fetch directory bytes and return them. ls formats the names and calls write; the kernel sends the bytes to the terminal. ls exits; the kernel notifies bash; bash prints the next prompt.
examples.answer: bash and ls are the two user processes; parsing, formatting and printing happen in user mode, while fork, execve, open, read, write and process creation run in kernel mode.

traps: The shell is not the kernel. bash is a user program; the kernel is the privileged core.
cd cannot be an external program. It changes the shell's own current directory, so it must be a built-in.

A utility, a shell built-in and a system call are different: ls is a utility, cd is a built-in, and getpid or write(2) is a system call; bash also has a built-in called read, which is not the read(2) system call.
fork and execve are not the same: fork copies a process; execve replaces its memory image.
User mode does not mean no kernel work: every file read crosses into kernel mode through a system call.

quiz.a: Kernel: privileged core that manages CPU, memory, drivers and system calls. User space: unprivileged memory where shells, utilities and applications run.

quiz.q: What is a system call? Give two examples.
quiz.a: A controlled entry from user mode to kernel mode; examples are open and read(2).

quiz.q: Why is cd a shell built-in and not a separate program?
quiz.a: cd changes the shell's own current directory. A child process would change its own copy and exit, leaving the parent shell's directory unchanged.

quiz.q: What do fork and execve do in the ls trace?
quiz.a: fork creates a child process; execve replaces the child's memory image with /bin/ls.

quiz.q: A user types date in bash. List the main steps and the mode of each. Name the user processes.
quiz.a: bash reads and parses (user); fork (kernel); execve (kernel); date runs and calls write (user, then kernel for terminal); date exits. User processes: bash and date.

quiz.q: A program reads a 1 MB file one byte per read instead of 4096 bytes per read. Analyze the effect on mode switches and time.
quiz.a: One-byte reads need about 1,048,576 system calls; 4096-byte reads need 256. Each call switches modes, so the byte-by-byte version pays far more overhead and is slower.

quiz.q: Why can a faulty editor crash itself but not the kernel, while a faulty driver can crash the kernel?
quiz.a: The editor runs in user mode with restricted memory; the kernel can kill it. A driver runs in kernel mode with full privileges, so its bug can corrupt kernel data.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems use the same boundary for containers: namespaces limit what a process sees, and seccomp filters which system calls it may make. Security research studies the system-call interface because it is the widest gate into the kernel. Search for seccomp, eBPF and system-call filtering to go further.
